newsitem.title: USA: How Schwinn bike company pedaled into bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: How Schwinn bike company pedaled into bankruptcy.

text.p: For generations, there were bicycles -- and there were Schwinns.

The company that built the bikes in Chicago was proudly independent, run by descendants of its German-born founder, until the fourth generation of Schwinns to control the company rode it into bankruptcy.
Two Chicago business journalists have chronicled the firm's fortunes in a new book, "No Hands: The rise and fall of the Schwinn Bicycle Company, an American institution."
The book, by Judith Crown and Glenn Coleman, traces the company back to its origins in the 1890s, when America was swept by a sudden bicycling craze.

"Just when millions of Americans had the wealth, time and inclination to pursue outdoor leisure activities," the authors write, "suddenly there was a vehicle that anyone could ride, anywhere, anytime."
Ignaz Schwinn, the son of a German piano and organ maker, emigrated to America, arriving in the booming manufacturing centre of Chicago in 1891. Within a few years he was producing his own bicycles.

By 1899, some 10 million cyclists were on the road nationwide. As bicycle manufacturing boomed, other businesses suffered. Piano sales plunged, taverns and theatres emptied out. Barbershop customers stopped coming in for a daily shave -- they were out bicycling instead.

The Schwinn company prospered for decades, but it all started to come apart in the 1970s and '80s. The company tried to cut costs and expand markets by shifting production to Mississippi, Hungary, Taiwan and mainland China. All the moves produced new headaches.

"Schwinn had two overarching problems," co-author Judith Crown said in an interview. "The first was complacency. In the 1960s and '70s the bicycle industry saw new imports, BMX bikes (sporting bike), mountain bikes, but Schwinn was turning up its nose at anything new and resting on its laurels."
Schwinn's other problem, Crown said, was its insistence on keeping ownership and control of the company in the family.
"The later generations grew up in totally different circumstances. They just didn't have the same focus and hunger," Crown said.

"When Schwinn reached the fourth generation of management, it was running on borrowed time," the authors write. "Studies show that only 10 percent of family-owned companies survive even the third generation."
Compounding Schwinn's problem, she said, was an unusual trust arrangement that ensured the company would be governed by primogeniture.

"It was a crazy structure that concentrated power in one side of the family," Crown said. "There was no way to let in any fresh air, and Schwinn suffocated because of that. They were unwilling to bring in outside investors, but as a small business they just didn't have the resources to do what they needed."

Schwinn was also slow to respond to changes in its market, the authors say. After decades of catering to children, the company failed to notice that by the mid-1980s half of all dealer bike sales were to adults who wanted sophisticated lightweight bikes that Schwinn didn't make.

Schwinn's share of the U.S. market, which exceeded 25 percent in 1950, eroded to 12 percent by 1979 and 5 percent in 1992. That year Schwinn, deep in debt and with no prospects of recovering, filed for bankruptcy.

The company passed into the hands of Sam Zell, a Chicago financier noted for unorthodox investments and an iconoclastic "bad boy" image. Zell, the authors report, called Schwinn "an extraordinary nameplate with an extraordinary franchise that was allowed to deteriorate."
Zell moved the company to the outdoor-sports mecca of Boulder, Colo. "The company is now doing well and is trying to cultivate a super-hip racing image," Crown said.
After the bankruptcy, the authors report, Edward Schwinn Jr., the last Schwinn to run the company, moved to the resort town of Lake Geneva, Wis.
There, he and a partner bought a cheese shop and mail-order business that sells gift baskets, jams and jellies, pickled vegetables and wax-coated cheeses in the shape of cows.
The revamped Schwinn company is a strong No. 2 in the independent dealer market in the United States, making some 500,000 bikes a year, about half as many as the current leader, Wisconsin-based Trek.
In 1994, Schwinn gamely celebrated the 100th anniversary of its founding with a "SchwinnDig" at a Las Vegas event that featured 100 cycling Elvis Presley imitators.
